::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- explain **boosting** as fitting small trees **sequentially** to the residuals of the current model, and implement it from scratch with stumps;
- describe how the **learning rate**, the **number of trees**, the **tree depth** and **early stopping** interact;
- define **pseudo-residuals** as the **negative gradient** of the loss, and compute them for squared error and log-loss;
- specify and tune an XGBoost model with `boost_tree()` in tidymodels, and read its variable importance;
- recognise the main XGBoost hyperparameters in the native `xgboost` R interface.
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidymodels)
library(xgboost)   # engine for boosted trees
```
:::


## 1. Why boosting?

A [random forest](46-random-forests.qmd) grows hundreds of large trees **independently** and averages them. Each tree is a complete, low-bias model; averaging removes part of their variance.

Boosting takes the opposite route. Think of a student revising for an exam with a set of practice questions. After the first attempt she does not start from scratch: she looks at the questions she got **wrong** and studies those. After the second attempt, again, she concentrates on what is still wrong. Each round of study is small, but each one is aimed at the remaining mistakes.

A boosted model is built in the same way:

1. start with a very simple prediction (for example, the mean of $y$);
2. look at the **residuals** — what the current model still gets wrong;
3. fit a **small tree** to those residuals;
4. add a **fraction** of that tree to the model, and go back to step 2.

Each tree on its own is a weak model (often just a few splits). Added together, hundreds of them can approximate complicated functions. Boosted trees — in implementations such as **XGBoost**, LightGBM and CatBoost — are among the most widely used methods for tabular data.

## 2. Boosting from scratch with stumps

### A toy problem

We reuse the simulated world of [the ML workflow lesson](44-ml-workflow.qmd): $y = \sin(2\pi x) + \varepsilon$ with noise standard deviation 0.3. We draw a training set, a validation set (to choose the number of trees) and a large test set (to see the truth).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
f_true <- function(x) sin(2 * pi * x)
sim_data <- function(n, sd = 0.3) {
  x <- runif(n)
  data.frame(x = x, y = f_true(x) + rnorm(n, sd = sd))
}
set.seed(47)
train <- sim_data(100)
valid <- sim_data(100)
test  <- sim_data(2000)
```
:::


### The weak learner: a stump

A **stump** is a tree with a single split: one threshold, two leaves, each predicting the mean of its observations. It is the same search as the regression split of the [decision-tree lesson](45-decision-trees.qmd), written as a function that returns the threshold and the two leaf values.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_stump <- function(x, r) {
  xs <- sort(unique(x))
  cuts <- (head(xs, -1) + tail(xs, -1)) / 2        # candidate thresholds
  sse <- vapply(cuts, \(s) {
    left <- r[x < s]
    right <- r[x >= s]
    sum((left - mean(left))^2) + sum((right - mean(right))^2)
  }, numeric(1))
  s <- cuts[which.min(sse)]
  list(cut = s, left = mean(r[x < s]), right = mean(r[x >= s]))
}
predict_stump <- function(stump, x) {
  ifelse(x < stump$cut, stump$left, stump$right)
}
```
:::


Before using it, let us check it. A stump with threshold $s$ is the same as a linear regression on the indicator $x \ge s$, so its fitted values must coincide with those of `lm()`:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
st <- fit_stump(train$x, train$y)
st
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> $cut
#> [1] 0.5304
#> 
#> $left
#> [1] 0.6037
#> 
#> $right
#> [1] -0.6272
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
check <- lm(y ~ I(x >= st$cut), data = train)
all.equal(unname(fitted(check)), predict_stump(st, train$x))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


The first stump splits at $x \approx$ 0.53 — roughly where the sine wave crosses zero — and predicts 0.6 on the left and -0.63 on the right. It is a very crude model of a sine wave.

### The boosting loop


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
boost_stumps <- function(x, y, n_trees, learn_rate) {
  f0 <- mean(y)                                     # starting prediction
  pred <- rep(f0, length(y))
  stumps <- vector("list", n_trees)
  for (m in seq_len(n_trees)) {
    r <- y - pred                                   # current residuals
    stumps[[m]] <- fit_stump(x, r)                  # stump fitted to them
    pred <- pred + learn_rate * predict_stump(stumps[[m]], x)
  }
  list(f0 = f0, stumps = stumps, learn_rate = learn_rate)
}
predict_boost <- function(model, x, n_trees = length(model$stumps)) {
  pred <- rep(model$f0, length(x))
  for (m in seq_len(n_trees)) {
    pred <- pred + model$learn_rate * predict_stump(model$stumps[[m]], x)
  }
  pred
}
```
:::


The whole algorithm is the `for` loop in `boost_stumps()`: compute the residuals, fit a stump to them, add a fraction `learn_rate` of the stump. The final model is the starting value plus the sum of all the shrunken stumps:

$$
\hat f(x) = f_0 + \nu \sum_{m=1}^{M} T_m(x),
$$

where $T_m$ is the $m$-th stump, $M$ the number of trees and $\nu$ the **learning rate**.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
boost_01 <- boost_stumps(train$x, train$y, n_trees = 200, learn_rate = 0.1)
x_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 400)
steps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 5, 25, 200), \(m) {
  data.frame(trees = paste(m, "trees"), x = x_grid,
             pred = predict_boost(boost_01, x_grid, n_trees = m))
}))
steps$trees <- factor(steps$trees, levels = unique(steps$trees))

ggplot(steps, aes(x, pred)) +
  geom_point(data = train, aes(x, y), colour = "grey60", size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = f_true(x)), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ trees) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "Prediction")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Boosted stumps (learning rate 0.1) after 1, 5, 25 and 200 trees. Grey points: training data; dashed line: the true curve.](47-gradient-boosting_files/figure-html/fig-boost-steps-1.png){#fig-boost-steps fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- After **1 tree**, the model is the overall mean plus one-tenth of the first stump: almost flat. With a learning rate of 0.1 each tree moves the prediction only a little.
- After **5 and 25 trees**, the step function starts to follow the wave: each new stump has been placed where the previous model was most wrong.
- After **200 trees**, the prediction is a staircase with many small steps that tracks the true curve closely. Every step comes from a stump; the sum of many crude pieces is a flexible function.
:::

## 3. Learning rate, number of trees and early stopping

Two hyperparameters work together:

- the **learning rate** $\nu$ (also called *shrinkage* or `eta`): how much of each new tree we add;
- the **number of trees** $M$.

With a large learning rate, each tree makes a big correction and the model fits the training data quickly — but also starts fitting the noise quickly. With a small learning rate, many more trees are needed, but the path is smoother. Let us record the error after every tree for four learning rates:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
rmse <- function(obs, pred) sqrt(mean((obs - pred)^2))
error_path <- function(model, x, y) {
  pred <- rep(model$f0, length(x))
  err <- numeric(length(model$stumps))
  for (m in seq_along(model$stumps)) {
    pred <- pred + model$learn_rate * predict_stump(model$stumps[[m]], x)
    err[m] <- rmse(y, pred)
  }
  err
}

paths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 0.3, 0.1, 0.03), \(lr) {
  mod <- boost_stumps(train$x, train$y, n_trees = 500, learn_rate = lr)
  data.frame(learn_rate = lr, tree = 1:500,
             train = error_path(mod, train$x, train$y),
             valid = error_path(mod, valid$x, valid$y))
}))
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
paths |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(train, valid), names_to = "data",
                      values_to = "rmse") |>
  ggplot(aes(tree, rmse, colour = factor(learn_rate), linetype = data)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.3, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(train = "dotted", valid = "solid")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.8)) +
  labs(x = "Number of trees (log scale)", y = "RMSE",
       colour = "Learning rate", linetype = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Training (dotted) and validation (solid) RMSE after each tree, for four learning rates. The dashed horizontal line is the noise level 0.3.](47-gradient-boosting_files/figure-html/fig-learning-rate-1.png){#fig-learning-rate fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
best_by_rate <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(paths, paths$learn_rate), \(d) {
  data.frame(learn_rate = d$learn_rate[1],
             best_trees = which.min(d$valid),
             best_valid = min(d$valid),
             valid_500 = d$valid[500],
             train_500 = d$train[500])
}))
best_by_rate
```

```

#> 0.03       0.03        500     0.3490    0.3490    0.2394
#> 0.1        0.10        295     0.3431    0.3471    0.2186
#> 0.3        0.30         92     0.3410    0.3612    0.1860
#> 1          1.00         33     0.3497    0.3810    0.1063
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

These curves are **learning curves**: error as a function of how long the model has been trained.

- The **training** error (dotted) only goes down. With learning rate 1 it reaches 0.11 after 500 trees — far below the noise level of 0.3, which means the model is memorising noise.
- The **validation** error (solid) first goes down, reaches a minimum and then slowly rises: more trees eventually mean **overfitting**. Unlike a random forest, a boosted model *can* overfit by adding trees.
- The smaller the learning rate, the later the minimum: 33 trees for learning rate 1, 295 for 0.1. With 0.03, 500 trees are not even enough to reach it.
- The best validation errors (`best_valid`) are similar across learning rates; the large rate 1 does slightly worse (0.35 against 0.341 for the best rate), because each of its steps is too coarse. A common practical rule: **use a small learning rate (0.01–0.1) and enough trees**, and let the data choose the number of trees.
:::

### Early stopping

Instead of fixing the number of trees in advance, we can keep adding trees and **stop when the validation error has not improved for a given number of rounds** (the *patience*). The model keeps the trees up to the best round.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
early_stop <- function(valid_error, patience) {
  best <- 1
  for (m in seq_along(valid_error)) {
    if (valid_error[m] < valid_error[best]) best <- m
    if (m - best >= patience) break             # no improvement for a while
  }
  c(best = best, stopped_at = m)
}
early_stop(paths$valid[paths$learn_rate == 0.1], patience = 20)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>       best stopped_at 
#>        295        315
```


:::
:::


With learning rate 0.1 and a patience of 20 rounds, training would stop after 315 trees and keep the first 295. Early stopping saves computing time and acts as a regulariser. Note that the validation data are now used to make a decision: they are part of the model-building process, and the final performance must still be measured on separate test data.

### Tree depth

We used stumps (depth 1). Deeper trees capture **interactions**: a stump splits on one variable at a time, so a sum of stumps is an *additive* model, $f(x) = f_1(x_1) + f_2(x_2) + \dots$. A depth-2 tree can represent "the effect of age depends on sex"; depth $d$ allows interactions among up to $d$ variables. Boosted trees are usually **shallow** (depth 1–8): deep trees would make each step too big and fit noise. With one predictor, as here, depth only changes how many steps each tree adds.

## 4. Why "gradient" boosting?

So far we fitted each tree to the ordinary residuals $y_i - \hat f(x_i)$. That is right for squared-error loss, but for a 0/1 outcome (did the passenger survive?) the model predicts a **log-odds** $F(x)$, and $y - F$ makes no sense. Gradient boosting generalises the idea.

Let $L(y, F)$ be the **loss** — how bad a prediction $F$ is when the truth is $y$. For each observation, ask: *in which direction should I move the current prediction $F_i$ to reduce the loss fastest?* The answer is the **negative gradient** (negative derivative) of the loss with respect to the prediction. These numbers are the **pseudo-residuals**:

$$
r_{i} = -\left.\frac{\partial L(y_i, F)}{\partial F}\right|_{F = \hat F_{m-1}(x_i)} .
$$

Each new tree is fitted to the pseudo-residuals, so boosting is **gradient descent in the space of functions**: every tree is a small step downhill.

| Loss | $L(y, F)$ | Pseudo-residual $-\partial L / \partial F$ |
|---|---|---|
| Squared error ($y$ numeric) | $\tfrac12 (y - F)^2$ | $y - F$ — the ordinary residual |
| Log-loss ($y \in \{0,1\}$, $p = 1/(1+e^{-F})$) | $-[y \log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)]$ | $y - p$ — observed minus predicted probability |

(The old version of this lesson wrote the pseudo-residual as minus the loss itself, $-L(y_i, F)$, forgetting the derivative: that quantity is always negative and does not point in a useful direction.)

We can check the log-loss row numerically, approximating the derivative with a small finite difference:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
log_loss <- function(y, f) {
  p <- plogis(f)                                 # log-odds -> probability
  -(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p))
}
y <- c(1, 0, 1)
f <- c(-2, 0, 1.5)                               # current log-odds
h <- 1e-6
numeric_grad <- (log_loss(y, f + h) - log_loss(y, f - h)) / (2 * h)
cbind(minus_gradient = -numeric_grad, y_minus_p = y - plogis(f))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>      minus_gradient y_minus_p
#> [1,]         0.8808    0.8808
#> [2,]        -0.5000   -0.5000
#> [3,]         0.1824    0.1824
```


:::
:::


The two columns agree. For the first passenger (survived, but predicted log-odds −2, i.e. $p \approx$ 0.12) the pseudo-residual is large and positive: the next tree will push that prediction up.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: the algorithm and what XGBoost adds

**Gradient boosting** (Friedman, 2001) with loss $L$, $M$ trees and learning rate $\nu$:

1. $\hat F_0(x) = \arg\min_c \sum_i L(y_i, c)$ (the mean for squared error, the log-odds of the overall proportion for log-loss).
2. For $m = 1, \dots, M$:
   a. $r_{im} = -\partial L(y_i, F)/\partial F$ at $F = \hat F_{m-1}(x_i)$;
   b. fit a regression tree with $J$ leaves to $(x_i, r_{im})$, giving regions $R_{jm}$;
   c. in each leaf choose $\gamma_{jm} = \arg\min_\gamma \sum_{x_i \in R_{jm}} L(y_i, \hat F_{m-1}(x_i) + \gamma)$;
   d. $\hat F_m(x) = \hat F_{m-1}(x) + \nu \sum_j \gamma_{jm} \mathbf 1(x \in R_{jm})$.

For squared error, step (c) gives the leaf mean of the residuals — exactly our `fit_stump()`.

**XGBoost** (Chen & Guestrin, 2016) uses a second-order (Newton) approximation of the loss, with gradients $g_i$ and second derivatives $h_i$ (for log-loss, $h_i = p_i(1 - p_i)$), and adds a penalty on each tree,
$$
\Omega(T) = \gamma\, J + \tfrac12 \lambda \sum_{j=1}^J w_j^2 \;(+\, \alpha \textstyle\sum_j |w_j|),
$$
where $w_j$ are the leaf values. The optimal leaf value is $w_j = -\sum_{i \in j} g_i / (\sum_{i \in j} h_i + \lambda)$, and a split is made only if it reduces the penalised loss by more than $\gamma$ (`loss_reduction` in tidymodels). Row subsampling (`sample_size`) and column subsampling (`mtry`) add randomness, as in a random forest, which usually reduces variance further (*stochastic* gradient boosting).
:::

## 5. XGBoost hyperparameters

The tidymodels function `boost_tree()` uses the same argument names for every engine. With `set_engine("xgboost")` they map to XGBoost parameters as follows:

| `boost_tree()` argument | XGBoost name | What it controls | Typical range |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trees` | `nrounds` | Maximum number of trees $M$ | 100 – 2000 (with early stopping) |
| `learn_rate` | `eta` | Shrinkage $\nu$ of each tree | 0.01 – 0.3 |
| `tree_depth` | `max_depth` | Depth of each tree (interaction order) | 1 – 8 |
| `min_n` | `min_child_weight` | Minimum (Hessian-weighted) size of a leaf | 1 – 40 |
| `loss_reduction` | `gamma` | Minimum loss reduction needed to split ($\gamma$) | 0 – 10 |
| `sample_size` | `subsample` | Fraction of rows used for each tree | 0.5 – 1 |
| `mtry` | `colsample_bynode` | Predictors considered at each split | a few to all |
| `stop_iter` | `early_stopping_rounds` | Patience for early stopping | 10 – 50 |

Other XGBoost parameters can be passed as **engine arguments**, e.g. `set_engine("xgboost", lambda = 1, alpha = 0)` for the L2 and L1 penalties on leaf values, `scale_pos_weight` to up-weight a rare positive class, or `device = "cuda"` to train on an NVIDIA GPU (the old `tree_method = "gpu_hist"` is deprecated).

## 6. Boosting the Titanic

We use the same Titanic preparation as in [the ML workflow lesson](44-ml-workflow.qmd):


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
titanic <- readr::read_csv(data_path("titanic_data.csv"),
                           na = c("", "NA", "?"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(survived, pclass, sex, age, sibsp, parch, fare, embarked) |>
  mutate(
    survived = factor(survived, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("yes", "no")),
    pclass   = factor(pclass, levels = 1:3, labels = c("1st", "2nd", "3rd")),
    sex      = factor(sex),
    embarked = factor(embarked)
  )

set.seed(2026)
titanic_split <- initial_split(titanic, prop = 0.75, strata = survived)
titanic_train <- training(titanic_split)
titanic_test  <- testing(titanic_split)
set.seed(2026)
titanic_folds <- vfold_cv(titanic_train, v = 5, strata = survived)
titanic_metrics <- metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity,
                              brier_class, mn_log_loss)
```
:::


### Recipe

XGBoost needs **numeric** predictors, so factors must become dummy variables. Trees are not affected by monotone transformations, so there is no need to log `fare` or to normalise. (XGBoost can handle missing values itself; we impute anyway, to keep the pipeline the same as for the other models.)


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
xgb_rec <- recipe(survived ~ ., data = titanic_train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())
```
:::


Unlike the old version of this lesson, we do not include both `fare` and a log-transformed copy of it (for trees they carry exactly the same information), and we do not invent an indicator "age < 18" and call it an interaction: trees of depth ≥ 2 find interactions by themselves.

### Model specification and tuning


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
xgb_spec <- boost_tree(
  trees = 1000, tree_depth = tune(), learn_rate = tune(),
  min_n = 5, loss_reduction = 0, sample_size = 0.8, mtry = 6,
  stop_iter = 20
) |>
  set_engine("xgboost", validation = 0.2) |>
  set_mode("classification")

xgb_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(xgb_rec) |>
  add_model(xgb_spec)
```
:::


- `trees = 1000` is only an **upper limit**: `stop_iter = 20` stops training when the log-loss on a validation set has not improved for 20 rounds.
- `validation = 0.2` is an engine argument: inside every fit, 20% of the (analysis) data are held out to monitor early stopping. Without it, the monitoring would be done on the training data themselves, where the loss keeps decreasing, so early stopping would hardly ever trigger.
- `sample_size = 0.8` uses a random 80% of the rows for each tree; `mtry = 6` considers 6 of the 9 dummy-coded predictors at each split.

We tune only depth and learning rate, on a deliberately small grid:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
xgb_grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(tree_depth = c(1L, 3L, 6L),
                               learn_rate = c(0.01, 0.05, 0.2))

set.seed(2026)
xgb_res <- tune_grid(xgb_wf, resamples = titanic_folds, grid = xgb_grid,
                     metrics = titanic_metrics)
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
autoplot(xgb_res, metric = c("roc_auc", "brier_class"))
```

## How to read this output

- Each line in the plot is one tree depth; the x-axis is the learning rate (on a log scale). Because of early stopping, a small learning rate is compensated by more trees, so the curves are often rather flat.
- The best combination is depth 6 with learning rate 0.2. Look at `std_err` in `show_best()`: several combinations are usually within one standard error of the best, so the exact choice matters little.
- If depth 1 (stumps, an additive model) is as good as deeper trees, the data contain little evidence of interactions that the model can exploit.
:::


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
xgb_final <- xgb_wf |>
  finalize_workflow(best_xgb) |>
  last_fit(titanic_split, metrics = titanic_metrics)
collect_metrics(xgb_final)
```

## Box: faster tuning by racing

A full grid evaluates every combination on every fold. **Racing** (package `finetune`) evaluates all combinations on the first few folds and then drops those that are clearly worse, so the remaining folds are spent on promising candidates only:

```r
library(finetune)
set.seed(2026)
xgb_race <- tune_race_anova(xgb_wf, resamples = titanic_folds,
                            grid = xgb_grid, metrics = titanic_metrics,
                            control = control_race(verbose_elim = TRUE))
```

The interface is the same as `tune_grid()`, and the result can be used with `show_best()` and `select_best()` in the same way.
:::

## 7. Variable importance


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
xgb_final |>
  extract_fit_parsnip() |>
  plot_importance(n = 9)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![XGBoost gain importance of the tuned model.](47-gradient-boosting_files/figure-html/fig-vip-xgb-1.png){#fig-vip-xgb fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


`plot_importance()` — a small helper defined in the course file `_common.R` (the former `vip` package was archived from CRAN in 2025) — shows for XGBoost models the **gain**: the total improvement in the loss brought by the splits on each variable, relative to the total. It is the boosting analogue of the impurity importance of random forests, and it has the same weakness: variables with many possible split points (`age`, `fare`) can look more important than they are. The names are those of the dummy variables (`sex_male`, `pclass_X3rd`, …), because that is what the model sees. **Permutation importance**, computed on held-out data and on the original variables, is shown in [lesson 49](49-model-comparison.qmd).

A more detailed explanation of individual predictions uses **SHAP values**, which split each prediction into additive contributions of the predictors. They are beyond the scope of this course; the `shapviz` package and Molnar's *Interpretable Machine Learning* (see Further reading) are good starting points.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Box: the native `xgboost` R interface (version ≥ 2)

tidymodels calls the `xgboost` package for you. You may also meet code that uses it directly. Recent versions of the R package (2.x and 3.x) changed several names: in particular, the list of data sets monitored during training is now called **`evals`** (it used to be `watchlist`), and parameters are best built with `xgb.params()`. A minimal example, using the recipe to produce numeric matrices:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
inner <- initial_split(titanic_train, prop = 0.8, strata = survived)
rec_prep <- prep(xgb_rec, training = training(inner))
to_dmatrix <- function(df) {
  baked <- bake(rec_prep, new_data = df)
  xgb.DMatrix(data = as.matrix(select(baked, -survived)),
              label = as.integer(baked$survived == "yes"))
}
dtrain <- to_dmatrix(training(inner))
dvalid <- to_dmatrix(testing(inner))

bst <- xgb.train(
  params = xgb.params(objective = "binary:logistic", eval_metric = "logloss",
                      max_depth = 3, learning_rate = 0.05, subsample = 0.8),
  data = dtrain,
  nrounds = 1000,
  evals = list(train = dtrain, valid = dvalid),
  early_stopping_rounds = 20,
  verbose = 0
)
```
:::


- The label must be numeric 0/1, and the predictors a numeric matrix: here the recipe is estimated on the inner training part only, then applied to both parts.
- `early_stopping_rounds` monitors the **last** data set in `evals` (here `valid`).
- `predict(bst, dvalid)` returns predicted probabilities of the label 1 (survival).
- `xgb.cv()` performs k-fold cross-validation with the same arguments plus `nfold`.

Details differ between versions of the package; check `?xgb.train` and `?xgb.params` for the version you have installed. In this course, tidymodels is the recommended interface.
:::

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Using too many trees without early stopping.** Unlike forests, boosting overfits when $M$ grows. Use a validation set or CV to choose $M$.
2. **Tuning the learning rate and the number of trees separately.** They trade off: halving the learning rate roughly doubles the number of trees needed. Fix a small learning rate and let early stopping choose $M$, or tune them together.
3. **Monitoring early stopping on the training data.** The training loss always decreases, so training never stops. In tidymodels, set the `validation` engine argument.
4. **Writing the pseudo-residual as the loss.** It is the **negative derivative** of the loss with respect to the prediction ($y - p$ for log-loss), not the loss itself.
5. **Reading gain importance as definitive.** Like impurity importance it favours variables with many split points. Use permutation importance on held-out data for interpretation.
6. **Using outdated xgboost code.** `watchlist` → `evals`, `tree_method = "gpu_hist"` → `device = "cuda"`.
:::

## 8. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. What is the main difference between how a random forest and a boosted model use their trees?

A forest grows large trees **independently** (in parallel) and **averages** them to reduce variance. Boosting grows small trees **sequentially**, each fitted to the pseudo-residuals of the current model, and **adds** them up; it mainly reduces bias, step by step.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. The current model predicts $p = 0.9$ for a passenger who died ($y = 0$). What is the pseudo-residual under log-loss, and what will the next tree do?

$y - p = 0 - 0.9 = -0.9$. The next tree will tend to push this passenger's log-odds **down**, towards a lower survival probability.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. Why can a sum of stumps not represent an interaction between age and sex?

Each stump depends on a single variable, so a sum of stumps is a sum of one-variable functions, $f_1(\text{age}) + f_2(\text{sex}) + \dots$. An interaction means that the effect of age **depends on** sex, which needs at least one tree that splits on both, i.e. depth ≥ 2.
:::

## 9. Exercises

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — predict the output.** Without running it: what does `boost_stumps(train$x, train$y, n_trees = 1, learn_rate = 1)` predict, compared with a single stump fitted to `y`? Then check with `all.equal()`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Exactly the same. The model starts at $\bar y$; the first stump is fitted to $y - \bar y$, so its leaf values are the leaf means of $y$ minus $\bar y$; adding all of it (learning rate 1) gives back the leaf means of $y$.
```r
m1 <- boost_stumps(train$x, train$y, n_trees = 1, learn_rate = 1)
all.equal(predict_boost(m1, test$x),
          predict_stump(fit_stump(train$x, train$y), test$x))   # TRUE
```
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — patience.** Fit 500 boosted stumps with learning rate 0.3 and compute the validation error path. Apply `early_stop()` with patience 5, 20 and 50. How do the chosen number of trees and the corresponding **test** RMSE change?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
mod03 <- boost_stumps(train$x, train$y, n_trees = 500, learn_rate = 0.3)
v03 <- error_path(mod03, valid$x, valid$y)
t03 <- error_path(mod03, test$x, test$y)
sapply(c(5, 20, 50), \(p) {
  es <- early_stop(v03, p)
  c(es, test_rmse = t03[es["best"]])
})
```
With patience 5, training stops early at a local minimum (about 83 trees); patience 20 and 50 both find the minimum around 92 trees, at the cost of fitting more trees before stopping. The test RMSE is about 0.325 in all three cases: once the number of trees is in a reasonable range, the result is not very sensitive to the patience.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — debug the old lesson.** The old version of this lesson wrote the pseudo-residuals as $r_{im} = -L(y_i, F_{m-1}(x_i))$, and its "hyperparameter grid search" was

```r
param_grid <- expand.grid(max_depth = c(3, 4, 5), eta = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.15))
best_params <- param_grid[1, ]
```

Explain the two problems.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(1) The pseudo-residual is the **negative derivative** of the loss with respect to the current prediction, $-\partial L/\partial F$, not minus the loss. Minus the log-loss is always negative and says nothing about the direction in which the prediction should move; the correct value is $y_i - p_i$. (2) The "grid search" never fits anything: it builds a grid and takes its first row. A real search fits every combination on resamples and compares their performance, e.g. with `tune_grid()` as in section 6.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — boosting for a 0/1 outcome.** Modify `boost_stumps()` into `boost_logit()` for a 0/1 outcome: start from the log-odds of the overall proportion (`qlogis(mean(y01))`), and fit each stump to the pseudo-residuals $y - p$, where $p$ = `plogis()` of the current log-odds. Test it on simulated data with `x <- runif(300)` and `y <- rbinom(300, 1, plogis(3 * sin(2 * pi * x)))`, with 200 trees and learning rate 0.1. Compare the fitted probabilities with the true ones at a few values of $x$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
boost_logit <- function(x, y01, n_trees, learn_rate) {
  f0 <- qlogis(mean(y01))
  f <- rep(f0, length(y01))
  stumps <- vector("list", n_trees)
  for (m in seq_len(n_trees)) {
    r <- y01 - plogis(f)                  # negative gradient of log-loss
    stumps[[m]] <- fit_stump(x, r)
    f <- f + learn_rate * predict_stump(stumps[[m]], x)
  }
  list(f0 = f0, stumps = stumps, learn_rate = learn_rate)
}
set.seed(471)
xc <- runif(300)
yc <- rbinom(300, 1, plogis(3 * sin(2 * pi * xc)))
mc <- boost_logit(xc, yc, n_trees = 200, learn_rate = 0.1)
x0 <- c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9)
round(cbind(x0, fitted = plogis(predict_boost(mc, x0)),
            true = plogis(3 * sin(2 * pi * x0))), 2)
```
`predict_boost()` can be reused because it simply adds up the shrunken stumps (now on the log-odds scale). The fitted probabilities follow the true curve: high (about 0.8) for $x < 0.5$, low (about 0.16) for $x > 0.5$, though less extreme than the truth near 0.25 and 0.75 — with only 300 noisy 0/1 outcomes the model is shrunk towards the middle. Real implementations also use a Newton step for the leaf values (see Going deeper), which converges faster.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — tune more, carefully.** Extend the Titanic grid to also tune `min_n` (values 2 and 20) and `sample_size` (0.5 and 1). How many models are fitted in total by `tune_grid()` with 5 folds? Run it and compare the best ROC AUC with that of section 6: is the improvement larger than its standard error?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
The grid has $3 \times 3 \times 2 \times 2 = 36$ combinations, so $36 \times 5 = 180$ boosted models.
```r
xgb_spec2 <- xgb_spec |>
  set_args(min_n = tune(), sample_size = tune())
xgb_grid2 <- tidyr::expand_grid(tree_depth = c(1L, 3L, 6L),
                                learn_rate = c(0.01, 0.05, 0.2),
                                min_n = c(2L, 20L),
                                sample_size = c(0.5, 1))
set.seed(2026)
xgb_res2 <- tune_grid(xgb_wf |> update_model(xgb_spec2),
                      resamples = titanic_folds, grid = xgb_grid2,
                      metrics = titanic_metrics)
show_best(xgb_res2, metric = "roc_auc", n = 3)
show_best(xgb_res, metric = "roc_auc", n = 1)
```
Typically the best AUC changes only in the third decimal, well within one standard error: on this data set, depth and learning rate (with early stopping) matter more than the other parameters. A bigger grid also increases the risk of selecting a combination that is lucky on these particular folds.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Idea / function | What it does |
|---|---|
| Boosting | Sum of small trees, each fitted to the pseudo-residuals of the current model |
| Pseudo-residual $-\partial L/\partial F$ | $y - F$ for squared error, $y - p$ for log-loss |
| Learning rate $\nu$ (`learn_rate`) | Fraction of each tree added; small = slower but smoother |
| Number of trees (`trees`) + early stopping (`stop_iter`) | Stop when validation loss stops improving |
| Depth (`tree_depth`) | Order of interactions; boosting uses shallow trees |
| `boost_tree(...) \|> set_engine("xgboost", validation = 0.2)` | tidymodels XGBoost specification with an early-stopping set |
| `tune_grid()`, `select_best()`, `last_fit()` | Tune on CV folds, finalise, evaluate once on the test set |
| `plot_importance()` (course helper) | Gain importance (biased like impurity importance) |
| `xgb.train(params = xgb.params(...), evals = ...)` | Native xgboost interface (≥ 2) |

- Boosting reduces **bias** step by step; forests reduce **variance** by averaging.
- Boosted models **can overfit** by adding trees: always choose $M$ on validation data.
- Small learning rate + early stopping is a robust default.
- "Gradient" boosting means each tree is a step along the **negative gradient** of the loss.
